1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6.name: Slav Defence
1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6.background: Although it was analysed as early as 1590, it was not until the 1920s that it started to be explored extensively. The two Alekhine–Euwe World Championship matches of 1935 and 1937 gave it an exhaustive test, and Vladimir Kramnik played it in six of his eight games as Black in the 2006 World Championship.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3.strategy: The main line: develops the knight, guards d4 and e5 and commits White to nothing. White can still hold the tension on c4, release it with an exchange on d5 or prepare a central pawn break, so Black has to show its set-up first.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3.name: Slav Defence
1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3.strategy: Adds a second attacker on d5 and keeps the e4 push available. It also makes the natural ...Bf5 a mistake: cxd5 and Qb3 then hit b7 and d5 at once and win a pawn. Black has to choose between grabbing the c-pawn and building a sturdy pawn chain.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.cxd5.name: Slav Defence: Exchange Variation
1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.cxd5.background: Once described as "the system that takes the fun out of playing the Slav" for Black, it is often used as a drawing weapon.
1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.cxd5.strategy: Resolves the tension at once and leaves a symmetrical pawn structure with the c-file open to both sides. Black equalises without trouble, so White keeps only the extra move and a quiet game, often the choice when a draw is welcome.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.e4.name: Slav Defence: Diemer Gambit
1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.e4.strategy: Sacrifices the e-pawn for a broad centre and quick development. Black simply takes with ...dxe4 and is a pawn up, so White has to find enough compensation in development and central space.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.cxd5 cxd5.strategy: Retakes and keeps the pawn structure symmetrical, so the game hinges on who handles the quiet middlegame better. Recapturing with the queen is worse: Nc3 hits it at once, and White gains a tempo and a free hand in the centre.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.cxd5 Nf6.strategy: Declines to recapture and develops instead, hoping to win the pawn back with a lead in development. White simply takes on c6, and after ...Nxc6 Black is a pawn down with only quick development and open lines to show for it.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.cxd5 Qxd5.strategy: Recaptures with the queen too early. Nc3 hits it at once, and when it moves White has developed with a tempo and can build a broad pawn centre at leisure.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.cxd5 cxd5 4.Nc3.strategy: The main way to play the exchange: the knight develops with pressure on d5 and keeps the tension. White hopes the extra move tells; Black has to defend d5 and develop accurately to keep the symmetry.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.cxd5 cxd5 4.Bf4.strategy: Develops the bishop outside the pawn chain before e3 can shut it in, aiming at c7 and the e5 square. It puts no pressure on d5, so Black develops freely; White relies on the extra move and a smooth set-up rather than on a direct threat.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.cxd5 cxd5 4.Nf3.strategy: The quiet route: the knight guards d4 and e5 and keeps White's options open, heading for the fully symmetrical set-up in which every piece stands well. It is the safe choice, since Black gets an easy game and White little more than the extra move.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.cxd5 cxd5 4.Nc3 Nf6.strategy: Answers the pressure on d5 with a second defender and develops towards the e4 square. Black keeps the symmetry and a solid game, with no weaknesses for White to aim at.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.cxd5 cxd5 4.Nc3 Nc6.strategy: Develops the queen's knight at once, hitting d4 and covering e5, and leaves the king's knight free to choose its square. For now d5 is guarded by the queen alone, so Black must develop accurately; the symmetrical structure keeps the game level.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.cxd5 cxd5 4.Nc3 e6.strategy: Backs d5 with a pawn, so no piece has to defend it, but shuts the c8 bishop in behind the pawn. Solid and without weaknesses, though the bishop is Black's problem piece for a long time and White, with the extra move, chooses how to build up.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.cxd5 cxd5 4.Nc3 Nf6 5..strategy: Solid development: the knight guards d4 and heads for a quiet, symmetrical position in which every piece stands well. White keeps the extra move but the symmetry offers little more than a safe game; Black has nothing to fear but also little to attack.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.cxd5 cxd5 4.Nc3 Nf6 5..name: Slav Defence: Exchange Variation, Boor Attack
1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.cxd5 cxd5 4.Nc3 Nf6 5..strategy: Prepares e2-e4 to build a broad pawn centre and break the symmetry. The cost is development: the pawn takes f3 from the king's knight and opens the e1-h4 diagonal, so Black can strike at the centre first.

The most common way to play the exchange: the bishop comes out outside the pawn chain before e3 can close it in, and White keeps the choice of how to place the king's knight. It watches c7 and e5; Black must match it with accurate development to hold the symmetry.

Mirrors White's development and puts the knight where it attacks d4 and covers e5. Black keeps the symmetrical structure and has no weaknesses, so the game stays level and quiet unless White finds a way to use the extra move.

Defends d5 a second time with a pawn and opens the f8 bishop, but closes in the c8 bishop behind the e6 pawn. Solid and symmetrical, yet it gives up the chance to develop that bishop actively, and White keeps the freer game.

A waiting move: it takes b5 away from White's knight and keeps the choice of development open, with the c8 bishop still free. It does not bring out a piece, so Black must reach a sound set-up a tempo behind the mirrored one.

Develops the bishop outside the pawn chain before e3 can shut it in, taking the diagonal towards c7 and b8 and control of e5. It is the natural way to use the extra move, and Black has to decide how to match it.

Supports d4 and opens the f1 bishop for a solid set-up, but it shuts in the c1 bishop and lets Black develop ...Bg4, pinning the f3 knight to the queen. White keeps a sound centre but little pressure.

Develops the bishop to g5, pressing on the f6 knight, but the knight is guarded twice, so nothing is threatened and the bishop can be challenged by ...h6 or ...Ne4. Sound but second-rate, since it gives Black a tempo target.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.cxd5 cxd5 4.Nc3 Nf6 5..name: Slav Defence: Exchange Variation, Symmetrical Line
1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.cxd5 cxd5 4.Nc3 Nf6 5..strategy: Mirrors the bishop and completes a fully symmetrical position in which every piece is well placed and neither side has a target. Black has reached equality by simple means; whoever wants more than a draw has to unbalance the position.

Breaks the mirror on purpose: the pawn takes b5 away from White's knight and waits, so Black decides where the bishop goes once White commits. It spends a tempo on a move that does not develop, which is affordable in such a quiet position.

Defends d5 with a pawn and prepares to trade the dark-squared bishops by ...Bd6, but locks in the c8 bishop. Sound and simple, yet Black swaps the active bishop move of the symmetrical set-up for a passive one.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 Nf6.strategy: Develops with pressure on e4 and adds a second defender to d5, so Black meets the pressure without committing the e-pawn or taking on c4. White now decides what kind of game it becomes.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 dxc4.name: Slav Defence
1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 dxc4.background: Sometimes called the Argentinian Defence, it is more common after 3.Nc3 than after 3.Nf3.
1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 dxc4.strategy: A surprise weapon: Black takes the pawn at once and prepares to hold it with ...b5, where the pawn on c6 helps and a later ...b4 can chase the c3 knight. The price is the centre, which White is free to occupy.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 e5.name: Slav Defence: Winawer Countergambit
1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 e5.background: Introduced by Szymon Winawer in his game against Frank Marshall at Monte Carlo in 1901, it is rarely seen in high-level games.
1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 e5.strategy: A counter-gambit that sacrifices a pawn for quick development: after dxe5, ...d4 chases the c3 knight and Black usually regains the pawn. White stays ahead in development, so Black has to prove the sacrifice was worth it.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 dxc4 4.e4.name: Slav Defence: Slav Gambit, Alekhine Attack
1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 dxc4 4.e4.strategy: Builds a big pawn centre at once and leaves the c4 pawn for later. The cost is that the c3 knight loses e4 as a retreat square, which counts once Black's queenside pawns advance. White plays for space and the initiative, Black for queenside counterplay.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 dxc4 4.e3.strategy: Prepares to win the pawn back with the bishop and keeps e4 free as a retreat for the c3 knight. Black tries to hold the pawn by advancing on the queenside, and the fight is whether that advance outruns White's development.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 dxc4 4.a4.strategy: Stops ...b5 before it starts, so the c4 pawn cannot be held by force. But the move spends time on the wing and lets Black strike at the centre at once with ...e5, which equalises comfortably.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 dxc4 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops the knight and leaves the choice of centre for later, but it does not stop ...b5, so Black can hold on to the extra pawn for now. The position stays level, with White having to find compensation in development.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 e5 4.e4.name: Slav Defence: Winawer Countergambit, Anti-Winawer Gambit
1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 e5 4.e4.strategy: Hits the centre at once instead of taking on e5. Black takes on d4 and then on e4, but White regains both pawns with the queen and the knight, the queens come off and Black's king loses castling. The result is level, with White's centre gone.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 e5 4.dxe5.strategy: Takes the offered pawn. Black regains it only at the cost of time: the knight is driven back and White ends with more pieces developed and the calmer game. Taking is the principled answer, and it keeps a small, lasting edge.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 e5 4.cxd5.strategy: Clears the centre before deciding what to do with the e5 pawn, keeping every plan open: capture it, support d4 or build a pawn centre. Black has no difficulties, but the exchange gives away the slight edge that taking on e5 keeps.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 e5 4.e3.strategy: Declines the gambit by supporting d4; after ...exd4 and the recapture White has an open e-file and a healthy centre, but Black equalises without difficulty. Safe and solid, without the edge that taking the pawn keeps.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Nf3.strategy: The main line: develops the knight, guards d4 and e5 and keeps the c1 bishop free to come out before e3. White keeps maximum flexibility and lets Black commit first.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e3.strategy: Supports d4 and opens the f1 bishop's diagonal, so ...dxc4 simply allows Bxc4. The price is a shut-in bishop on c1 and a slower plan; White gets a solid centre and a flexible game rather than a quick initiative.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.cxd5.strategy: Relieves the tension at once and heads for a symmetrical pawn structure with the knight already on c3. It avoids the complications of the Slav but also gives up the central tension, and with it most of White's winning chances.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e3 e6.strategy: Backs up d5 solidly and keeps the kingside developing freely, at the price of closing in the c8 bishop for now. Black accepts a slightly passive bishop for a sturdy centre and later pawn breaks, while White's c1 bishop is hemmed in by e3 as well.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e3 g6.strategy: Prepares a kingside fianchetto and keeps the c8 bishop free instead of closing it in with ...e6. Sound but slower than the standard pawn chain: White gets time to build in the centre while the bishop on g7 waits behind its own knight.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e3 a6.strategy: A flexible waiting move: it takes b5 away from White's knight and prepares ...b5, so that a later capture on c4 can be held. Black keeps the choice between a solid and an open set-up, at the price of doing nothing yet in the centre.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e3 e6 5.Nf3.name: Semi-Slav Defence: Main Line
1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e3 e6 5.Nf3.strategy: Develops the knight, guards d4 and e5 and keeps the f1 bishop ready to recapture on c4. With e3 played, the dark-squared bishop is closed in and White heads for a solid central game rather than a pin on the f6 knight.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e3 e6 5.Bd3.strategy: Brings the bishop to its most active diagonal at once, aimed at h7, and keeps the choice of knight square. But Black can take on c4 immediately: after Bxc4 the push ...b5 chases the bishop back and Black gains queenside space with tempo.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e3 e6 5.Qb3.strategy: Guards c4 with the queen and eyes b7, so Black gains no tempo by taking on c4. But the queen is early and exposed and White's development lags, which lets Black finish developing and equalise without difficulty.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e3 e6 5.Nf3.name: Semi-Slav Defence: Normal Variation
1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e3 e6 5.Nf3.strategy: The standard developing move: the knight guards e5, covers b6 and supports the freeing breaks in the centre. Black accepts a compact, slightly cramped position with the c8 bishop still shut in, and waits for White to commit before choosing between a central break and queenside expansion.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e3 e6 5.Nf3.name: Semi-Slav Defence: Accelerated Meran Variation
1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e3 e6 5.Nf3.strategy: Prepares ...b5 in advance, so that a later ...dxc4 can be supported, and leaves the b8 knight free to choose its square. Black spends a tempo on the edge pawn but gains flexibility for queenside expansion.

Hits the c3 knight and offers a trade to ease Black's cramped position. The price is that White can recapture with the b-pawn and gain a strong centre, while Black has spent a second move with the same knight.

Puts the bishop on its natural diagonal, eyeing h2 and supporting an ...e5 break. Sound but second-rate: the bishop is committed before White shows a set-up, and with the c8 bishop still shut in, Black has done little about the real problem.

Develops the bishop to its best diagonal and invites Black to take the pawn. After the capture White retakes and plays for the central advance, while Black grabs queenside space with tempo on the bishop. A rich, double-edged game: White gets the centre, Black the queenside.

Claims space and closes the queenside, ruling out ...dxc4 and the queenside play that ...a6 prepared. Black's pieces lose room, but the advanced pawn becomes a target that Black can undermine from the flank, so White must support it.
Supports c4 with a pawn and prepares to develop the bishop on the long diagonal, keeping the tension in the centre. It spends a tempo on the wing, which gives Black time to complete development.

Takes the pawn and clears d5, giving up the centre for queenside expansion and time against the bishop. With ...a6 already played, the pawn push against the bishop is ready at once. Black then plays to free the c8-bishop by striking at White's centre.

Develops the bishop to its active diagonal, aimed at h2, and keeps the d5 pawn instead of giving up the centre for queenside space. Black prepares to castle and to break with ...e5, and accepts that White's bishop stays on its best square on d3.

Develops the queen's knight and supports ...e5 and ...c5, keeping the capture on c4 in reserve. But it blocks the c8 bishop and leaves White to decide the structure, whether by exchanging on d5 or by advancing in the centre.

Develops the bishop to its most active diagonal, aimed at h7, and prepares to castle. If Black takes on c4, the bishop must recapture there and White loses a tempo, but White accepts that to keep the centre and play for a long positional game.

Aims the queen along the b1-h7 diagonal and keeps the f1 bishop flexible: after ...dxc4 it recaptures in one move, with no tempo lost. The price is a slower build-up, since Black castles and prepares ...e5 without being hurried.

Supports c4 with a pawn and prepares the long diagonal for the c1 bishop, keeping the tension. It spends a move on the wing, and Black meanwhile castles and builds up with the bishop already aimed at h2.

Takes the pawn exactly when the bishop has committed to d3: it has to retake on c4, so White loses a tempo. Black gives up the d5-pawn's grip on the centre but gains time to free the position with a central pawn break.

Builds the compact centre, with pawns on d5 and e6, a bishop on d6 and knights on d7 and f6, and keeps ...dxc4 in reserve until it gains something. The c8 bishop stays shut in, so Black needs a central break to free it.

Gets the king to safety at once and leaves the capture on c4 for later, relying on the f6 knight to cover h7 against the bishop on d3. It does nothing about the tension on c4, so White can choose to exchange on d5 or push in the centre.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e3 e6 5.Nf3.name: Semi-Slav Defence: Main Line
1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e3 e6 5.Nf3.background: It provokes the Meran Variation (6...dxc4 7.Bxc4 b5), first played in 1906 in the game Schlechter–Perlis. The variation takes its name from the town of Meran, where a 1924 tournament saw it used successfully in the game Grünfeld–Rubinstein.
1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e3 e6 5.Nf3.strategy: Aims the bishop at the kingside and invites Black to open the centre: if Black takes on c4, the bishop recaptures and ...b5 gains time against it. White plays for a central e4 push, Black for queenside expansion in exchange for the centre; the game is sharp and double-edged.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e3 e6 5.Nf3.name: Semi-Slav Defence: Stoltz Variation
1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e3 e6 5.Nf3.background: Named after the Swedish grandmaster Gösta Stoltz, it was once a sideline and then exploded in popularity in the 1990s, in large part through Anatoly Karpov's advocacy.
1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e3 e6 5.Nf3.strategy: Waits before placing the bishop: the queen supports e4 and eyes h7 along the b1-h7 diagonal, and White decides where the bishop goes only once Black has committed to ...dxc4. The game is slower, with White keeping a flexible central structure.
Guards the c4 pawn so that ...dxc4 never wins it, and prepares the bishop on the long diagonal, although the c3 knight stands in its way. Slow: Black has time to complete development.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e3 e6 5.Nf3.name: Semi-Slav Defence: Rubinstein System
1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e3 e6 5.Nf3.strategy: Stakes out e5, pressing on d7 and f7. White spends a second move with the same knight without developing a new piece, and Black can challenge and trade it, so the gain of space is small.

Develops the bishop on its best diagonal, aiming at h2 and preparing castling and the ...e5 break. White's b3 has spent time on the queenside, so Black completes development and fights for the centre without problems.

Resolves the tension by taking: Black gets a clear plan against either recapture, a central break against the pawn centre after bxc4, or a queenside push against the bishop after Bxc4. It gives up the d5 pawn's hold on the centre, but White's b3 has already spent time on the wing.

Prepares to fianchetto the queen's bishop, but the c6 pawn blocks that bishop until ...c5, which gives up the compact centre. Playable, though slow: Black spends a tempo on a plan that only works after a pawn break.

Takes on c4 now that White's bishop has committed to d3: after Bxc4, ...b5 gains a tempo against it. Black trades the centre for queenside space and activity, while White gets a free hand in the middle; the result is a double-edged fight.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e3 e6 5.Nf3.name: Semi-Slav Defence: Chigorin Defence
1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e3 e6 5.Nf3.background: Much the most popular line before the Meran came into play, it was espoused by the American grandmaster Arthur Bisguier throughout his career.
1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e3 e6 5.Nf3.strategy: Supports the ...e5 break and eyes the h2 pawn, so that White's own central push can be answered at once. Black delays ...dxc4 and keeps more of the pawn centre.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e3 e6 5.Nf3.name: Semi-Slav Defence: Bogoljubow Variation
1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e3 e6 5.Nf3.strategy: Solid but passive: the bishop does nothing to prepare the ...e5 break, so White can build in the centre with little to fear. Black castles quickly but gets little counterplay.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e3 e6 5.Nf3.name: Semi-Slav Defence: Romih Variation
1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e3 e6 5.Nf3.background: Introduced by the Italian master Max Romih.
1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e3 e6 5.Nf3.strategy: Pins the c3 knight to the king, which holds back e4 for the moment. The pin is easily broken, and if Black trades on c3 White recaptures with the b-pawn and keeps the two bishops, so the move gains little.
Develops the bishop with an eye on h2 and supports the ...e5 break. Black does not take on c4 yet, so White's bishop has no target and Black stays flexible, with central counterplay as the main plan.

Prepares to bring the queen's bishop to b7, but that bishop is blocked by the c6 pawn until Black plays ...c5, which gives up the compact centre. The plan is slow and gives White time to build in the centre.
Solid and flexible, but passive: the bishop on e7 does not support the freeing ...e5 break or point at h2 as it does on d6, so Black has less counterplay. White can build up calmly.

Attacks the knight a second time: the c3 knight and the bishop both hit e4, defended only by the d5 pawn, so Black must support, trade or move it. If Black trades on c3, White recaptures towards the centre and gets a broad pawn centre at the price of doubled c-pawns.

Trades the intruding knight at once, but ...dxe4 attacks the f3 knight, which has to retreat, so Black gains a tempo and a pawn on e4 that cramps White's kingside. White can attack the pawn but Black can support it, so the trade gives White no edge.

Adds a second attacker to e4, so Black must trade on c3 or support the knight with ...f5, which weakens the king's side. The queen comes out early and the bishop stays flexible; the trade on c3 leaves White with a healthy centre.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e3 e6 5.Nf3.name: Semi-Slav Defence: Stonewall Defence
1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e3 e6 5.Nf3.strategy: Supports the knight on e4 with the f-pawn, building a wall of pawns on c6, d5, e6 and f5 and a firm outpost for the knight. The cost is lasting: the e5 square is left to White, and the c8-bishop stays shut in behind its own pawns.

The knight on e4 is attacked twice and held only by the d5 pawn, so Black trades it for the c3 knight. White must retake with the b-pawn, which doubles the c-pawns and loosens the queenside, in return for a broad centre that Black can strike at once.

Retreats the knight to where it started, which costs two moves for nothing. The structure is the quiet Semi-Slav chain again, but White has gained the useful Bd3 for free and can castle and prepare the centre at leisure.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e3 g6 5.Nf3.strategy: Develops the knight and guards d4 and e5, the squares a fianchettoed bishop on g7 will aim at. White keeps a compact centre and waits to see how Black's set-up develops.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e3 g6 5.Bd3.strategy: Defends c4 and prepares e4 and castling, but commits the bishop before the knight. Black can take on c4 and chase the recapturing bishop with ...b5, so White regains the pawn while Black gains queenside space.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e3 g6 5.cxd5.strategy: Settles the centre at once by exchanging the pawn that cramps Black's queenside. The game turns quiet and symmetrical, White's centre is only d4 and e3, and with the c-file opening White has little more than the first move's slight edge.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e3 g6 5.Nf3.strategy: Completes the fianchetto and prepares castling. The bishop aims at d4 along the long diagonal once the f6 knight moves, giving White's centre a long-term target, while the pawn chain on c6 and d5 stays solid.

Resolves the tension at once: White recaptures on c4, Black fianchettoes and castles, and the light-squared bishop gets out freely. White gains a broad centre with e4, and Black's fianchettoed bishop and a later ...c5 must challenge it.
Brings the last minor piece into play and supports a later central break, but it shuts in the c8 bishop. It waits rather than resolving the tension on c4, so White chooses how the centre is settled.
Develops the bishop where it guards c4 and supports a later e4, and prepares castling. White builds a classical set-up and neither side has committed in the centre.
Guards c4 and prepares castling from a modest square. The bishop is less active than on d3 and does not back an advance of the e-pawn, so White settles for a slower, solid build-up.

Exchanges at once and gives up the c4 pawn that cramps Black's queenside. Against the fianchetto set-up the game turns quiet and fairly symmetrical, without the tension that makes the Slav sharp, and White must find play on the open c-file.
Castles into safety and brings the rook towards the centre. The king and the fianchettoed bishop stand together, and Black can now turn to the centre and to the still undeveloped c8 bishop.

Takes the pawn so that White's bishop must recapture, then chases it with ...b5 to gain queenside space. Black gives up the central d5 pawn and lets White build an e4 centre, which the fianchettoed bishop and a later ...c5 must challenge.
Develops the last knight and guards e5 and b6 for later breaks, while Black keeps the choice of taking on c4. The king stays in the centre a move longer, which lets White open the centre first.
